title: Change detectives: what became something new?
subtitle: Evidence from a repair workshop
objective: Describe burning and rusting as changes that form new materials, and distinguish them from a change of state.

sow.exactOutcome: Describe irreversible changes (burning, rusting, new materials formed).
sow.alignment: Directly develops the stated outcome. Original teacher-authored exemplar; route support is responsive and not a qualification or fixed ability label.

priorLearning: Explain how salt can be recovered from a solution.
success: Use evidence to distinguish a new substance from a change of shape or state.
Explain why cooling burnt wood or rust does not restore the starting material.
Describe iron rusting and fuel burning without claiming that matter disappears.

vocabulary.meaning: A material with a particular chemical identity.
A change of form or state that does not make a new substance.
A change in which new substances are formed.
Iron reacting with oxygen and water to form rust.
A chemical reaction of a fuel with oxygen that transfers energy.
Not returned to the starting material by simply reversing the classroom process.

equipment: Shared evidence sheet, one selected response route and exit sheet; pencils.
preparation: Read the worked answers and preview the three interactive decisions.
Print shared page 1, one route from pages 2–4, and page 5.
safety: This lesson uses supplied evidence cards and diagrams. No flames, hot wax, chemicals or rusty sharp objects are needed.
If using a sample for looking, the teacher selects a clean sealed display; pupils do not scrape or handle corroded edges.
practicalAlternative: All observations are supplied as constructed teaching cases. The complete lesson is a desk investigation; pupils are not asked to make or burn materials.

misconceptions.claim: Anything difficult to undo is a chemical change.
misconceptions.correction: Tearing paper changes its form without necessarily making a new substance. New-substance evidence is the key.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether cutting paper creates a new substance.

misconceptions.claim: Wax melting and wax burning are the same change.
misconceptions.correction: Melting changes state; wax vapour burning reacts with oxygen to make new substances.

misconceptions.claim: Rust is iron with brown dirt on it.
misconceptions.correction: Rust contains new substances formed as iron reacts with oxygen and water.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether wiping or cooling turns rust into iron.

misconceptions.correction: Matter is rearranged into products, including gases that can escape into air.
misconceptions.check: Ask what an open tray fails to collect.

access.supported: Use short choices, named evidence cards and a sentence bank. Accept pointing followed by one spoken reason.
access.standard: Classify four cases and write an evidence-based repair label explaining new substances.
access.stretch: Evaluate a misleading irreversible-change rule and explain an open-system mass observation qualitatively.
access.regulation: Use fictional workshop cases. Offer private responses, drawing or scribing; pupils may pass and return to a shared question. No sensory smoke or flame exposure is part of the task.

slides.title: The workshop has mixed up its labels
body: A torn ticket and a rusty bracket both look different.
Did both become a new substance?
slides.notes: Frame a desk evidence investigation. Do not classify by dramatic appearance. Point to the difference between an object and the substance it is made from.

slides.title: Three things we can recover
body: R1. How could liquid water become ice?
R2. Does dissolved salt stop existing?
R3. Does melting always make a new substance?
slides.notes: R1 cool below freezing point. R2 no; it remains in solution and can be recovered. R3 no; state changes retain substance identity. Use responses to recap the preceding recovery lesson briefly.

slides.title: I ask two different questions
body: Can a simple process reverse this change?
Is the material still the same substance?
I use the second question to classify the change.
slides.notes: Think aloud: I can freeze melted ice; the substance is water throughout. A torn paper sheet is hard to restore, yet tearing has not by itself created a new substance. This is why “hard to undo” alone is an unreliable chemical test. Do not teach all physical changes as reversible.

visual.title: Two questions about a change
visual.description: Two separate questions distinguish reversibility from substance identity. Melting ice can be reversed by cooling and makes no new substance; tearing paper is difficult to reverse but also makes no new substance.

elements.text: Can we undo it? Did it make a new substance?

Cooling can reverse it.
The substance is still water.
Physical change.

Hard to restore the sheet.
The paper is still paper.
Physical change.

Being hard to undo is not enough evidence
that a new substance formed.

slides.title: I explain the rusty bracket
body: Iron reacts with oxygen and water.
Rust is a new material.
Cooling does not restore the original iron.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Use the word model as a relationship, not a particle picture or balanced equation. Rust is a mixture of iron oxides/hydroxides, often simplified as hydrated iron oxide; that name is not required. Ordinary rusting needs both oxygen and water. Salt can accelerate it but is not essential.

visual.title: Iron reacts to form rust
visual.description: A word model shows iron and oxygen with water forming rust; this is not a balanced equation and the shapes are labels, not particles.

elements.text:
Cooling or wiping rust does not make it iron again.
Word model: not a balanced chemical equation.
Rusting is gradual; animation time is not real time.

slides.title: I separate two candle processes
body: Melting wax changes its state.
Burning wax vapour makes new substances.
Cooling reverses melting, not burning.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Solid wax melts; liquid wax is drawn up a wick and vaporises before reacting. The top and bottom panels represent different changes, not a single arrow joining liquid wax directly to products. Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water; incomplete combustion can also produce soot and other products. No live demonstration.

visual.title: One candle, two different changes
visual.description: A top row shows reversible wax melting and solidifying. A separate bottom row shows wax vapour plus oxygen forming carbon dioxide and water; these chemical products are not turned back into wax by cooling.

elements.text:
Burning forms new substances. This word model
omits incomplete-combustion products.

slides.title: The evidence sorting board
body: Read cards A–D on shared page 1.
W1. Sort by whether new substances formed.
Give the evidence, not just a letter.
slides.notes: Use 3 minutes of We do: A/B physical; C/D chemical. For B explain same paper even though sheet restoration is difficult. C has analysis evidence; D identifies products. Each pupil commits a sort by pointing or noting letters before feedback.

slides.title: Repair the workshop rule
body: W2. Test the rule against torn paper.
Replace it with a better decision question.
Which case supports your new rule?
slides.notes: Use 2 minutes: torn paper is a counterexample. Better question: has evidence shown a new substance formed? C rust and D burning support it. A visual change is a clue, not sufficient proof of a chemical change.

slides.title: Two labels for one candle
body: W3. Label E-A and E-B separately.
Which part can cooling reverse?
Where does the burnt wax material go?
slides.notes: Use 3 minutes: E-A physical melting; E-B chemical burning. Cooling can solidify remaining liquid wax. Burnt wax reacts with oxygen, making products including gases; atoms do not vanish.
slides.reveal: Melting: state change. Burning: new substances, including gases.

slides.title: Which is the strongest evidence?
body: A sample looks different after a change.
Which fact most supports a chemical change?
slides.notes: A incorrect: shape can change physically. B correct: new-substance evidence. C incorrect: physical changes can be difficult to undo. If uncertain, return to torn paper and rusty iron, asking about substance identity.

options.feedback: A shape change can leave the substance unchanged.
Formation of a new substance defines a chemical change.

options.text: It is awkward to put back.
options.feedback: Torn paper can be awkward to restore without a chemical change.

slides.title: Write a workshop diagnosis
body: Choose one response route.
Classify with evidence and explain rusting or burning.
Make a label a younger visitor can understand.
slides.notes: Independent 10 minutes over three slides. Select support from hinge evidence. Offer the evidence sheet on all routes. Adult may read questions but must not provide classification or causal explanation.

slides.title: Use a cause, not only a description
body: “It turned brown” describes an observation.
What new material formed?
What reacted to produce it?
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Prompt the type of explanation without naming answers. Pupils can use labels and arrows instead of a paragraph.

slides.title: Check the two-change trap
body: Have you separated wax melting from burning?
Have you avoided “everything disappears”?
Use one accurate reason per diagnosis.
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Check task access only; do not read model answers until the independent attempt is complete.

slides.title: Audit the diagnosis
body: Share privately, with a partner, or with the teacher.
Underline the evidence for a new substance.
Correct one misleading rule.
slides.notes: Review after collecting independent evidence. Accept scientific meaning rather than prescribed wording. A correctly classified case without a reason is partial, not secure evidence.

slides.title: Choose the next exhibit
body: Should the workshop show rusting or candle changes?
Explain which would clear up a misconception.
We will use one reason to improve the display.
slides.notes: Lundy pupil voice: collect suggestions, select one improvement, and explain how pupil reasoning affected the teacher’s next explanation. Passing or submitting a written suggestion is valid.

slides.title: Leave a reliable label
body: E1. Why is rusting a chemical change?
E2. Why can torn paper still be physical?
E3. What is different about wax burning?
slides.notes: E1 new rust material forms from iron with oxygen/water. E2 no new substance just from tearing. E3 reaction forms new products, unlike state change. Collect before revealing answers.

pupilPages.title: 1 • Shared evidence: workshop cases
pupilPages.intro: Constructed teaching cases. Use these for W1–W3; no practical experiment is required.

cards.title: A • Ice tray
cards.text: Ice warms into liquid water. Cooling below its freezing point makes ice again.

cards.title: B • Paper ticket
cards.text: A ticket is torn into pieces. Tests identify the pieces as the same paper material.

cards.title: C • Iron bracket
cards.text: After days in moist air, a brown coating forms. Analysis identifies rust, a new material.

cards.title: D • Wood offcut
cards.text: Burning forms ash and gases. Cooling the products does not restore the wood.

cards.title: E • Candle wax
cards.text: A: solid wax melts. B: wax vapour burns with oxygen, forming carbon dioxide and water.

cards.title: Rule to audit
cards.text: “If I cannot put it back easily, it must be a chemical change.”

blocks.prompt: W1. Sort A–D: new substance / no new substance. Explain one choice.
W2. Repair the rule using case B.
W3. Classify E-A and E-B. Which change can cooling reverse?

pupilPages.title: 2 • Supported route: diagnosis cards
pupilPages.intro: Use page 1. Circle, label, draw or dictate. Word bank: oxygen / water / rust / new.

blocks.prompt: S1. Rusting makes …
S2. Complete: Iron reacts with ____ and ____ to form ____ .
S3. Melting ice is a physical change because …
choices: All changes involving heat are chemical

blocks.prompt: S4. Explain why tearing paper does not prove a chemical change.
S5. Write two candle labels: one for melting and one for burning. Include “new substance” in one label.

pupilPages.title: 3 • Standard route: repair report
pupilPages.intro: Use evidence, not just appearance. A short sentence or labelled diagram is enough.

blocks.prompt: N1. Complete the classification table.
N2. Explain why rusting is not reversed by simply cooling the bracket.
N3. A visitor says wax melting and burning are the same. Write a two-sentence correction.
N4. Explain why some products of burning are missing from an open tray.

pupilPages.title: 4 • Stretch route: test a tempting rule
pupilPages.intro: Two claims need careful correction. No chemical equation is required.

blocks.text: Claim A: “Every change that is hard to undo forms a new substance.” Claim B: “Only 2 g of ash remained from 10 g of dry wood, so 8 g of matter was destroyed.” These masses are a constructed teaching example from an open system.

blocks.prompt: T1. Use a counterexample to evaluate claim A. Give a better classification rule.
T2. Explain claim B’s error. Include gases and oxygen from the air. Why can we not calculate the total gas mass as simply 8 g?
T3. Design two contrasting exhibit labels for wax melting and burning, explaining the role of cooling.

pupilPages.title: 5 • Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Work independently. Use science words where helpful.

blocks.prompt: E1. Explain why rusting is a chemical change.
E2. Why can tearing paper be a physical change even if it is difficult to restore?
E3. Give one difference between wax melting and wax burning.
E4. Where can some burning products go in an open system?
Reflection. Which workshop claim would you now challenge, and why?

answers.label: R1–R3
answers.answer: R1 cool water below its freezing point. R2 salt remains present in solution and can be recovered. R3 no, melting is a state change.

answers.label: W1–W3
answers.answer: W1 A/B: no new substance, physical; C/D: new substances, chemical. W2 torn paper retains the same material even though the sheet is hard to restore; ask whether new substances formed. W3 E-A physical melting, E-B chemical burning; cooling can solidify remaining melted wax, but does not turn combustion products back into wax. Gaseous products enter the air.

answers.label: Hinge A–C
answers.answer: A incorrect: a shape change may be physical. B correct: new substance identified. C incorrect: difficulty reversing does not establish chemical change.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1 new material. S2 oxygen/water/rust. S3 substance still water. S4 tearing changes shape/size but does not itself make a new substance. S5 melting: solid to liquid, same wax, cooling reverses it; burning: wax vapour reacts with oxygen to make new substances such as carbon dioxide and water.

answers.label: N1–N4
answers.answer: N1 ice physical/same water; paper physical/same paper; iron chemical/new rust; wood chemical/new ash and gases. N2 rust is a chemically different material; cooling does not undo that reaction. N3 melting changes wax’s state; burning wax vapour reacts with oxygen and produces new substances. N4 gases spread into the surrounding air; the open tray does not collect all products.

answers.label: T1–T3
answers.answer: T1 torn paper is a valid counterexample; a physical change can be hard to reverse. Look for formation of new substances. T2 gases escaped and oxygen entered from the air as a reactant. Matter was rearranged, not destroyed. The original wood mass excludes the incoming oxygen, so total gas product mass cannot be obtained as 10−2 alone. T3 separate accurate labels: melting is state change and liquid wax can solidify; burning makes new products and cooling does not restore wax. Accept accurate mention of incomplete-combustion products.

answers.label: E1–E4 / reflection
answers.answer: E1 rusting forms new substances as iron reacts with oxygen and water. E2 same paper material remains. E3 melting changes state, burning forms new substances. E4 into the surrounding air as gases; ash may remain. Reflection accepts any correctly justified correction.

answers.label: Evidence and responsive teaching
answers.answer: Secure core evidence: classifies both rusting and burning using new-substance reasoning and distinguishes melting from burning. Developing: classification is correct but relies only on appearance or difficulty reversing. Re-teach with the ice/paper contrast and the two separate candle processes. Stretch open-system mass reasoning is optional and must not become a core barrier.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 8; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 10; review 4; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Print shared page 1, ONE selected response route (2, 3 or 4), and exit page 5. Do not require all routes. Adult scribing records the pupil’s own words.
The SOW term “irreversible” refers to everyday classroom reversal, not a universal rule that all chemical reactions are irreversible. Do not extend the shortcut to torn paper.
Salt is not essential for rusting; ordinary rusting requires oxygen and water. The lesson uses supplied analysis rather than treating a colour change alone as proof.
All masses and workshop events are constructed illustrations, not collected school observations. No home burning task is suggested.

interactive.title: The workshop evidence board
interactive.intro: Choose a prediction, test the diagram, then explain. Pause or reset at any time. Paper W1–W3 use the same evidence.

steps.question: Which pair makes no new substance in our cases?

choices.text: A ice and B torn paper
choices.feedback: Both change form/state while retaining the same substance.

choices.text: B torn paper and C rusty iron
choices.feedback: Rust is a new material; tearing alone is a physical change.

choices.text: C rusty iron and D burning wood
choices.feedback: Both involve formation of new substances.

steps.question: Which explanation best fits the rusty bracket?

choices.text: Iron reacted with oxygen and water.
choices.feedback: The reaction forms rust, a new material.

choices.text: The iron only froze into a brown shape.
choices.feedback: Rusting is a chemical change, not freezing.

choices.text: Water painted the original iron brown.
choices.feedback: The coating contains newly formed rust substances.

visual.description: A word model shows iron and oxygen with water forming rust; this is not a balanced equation and the shapes are labels, not particles.

elements.text:
Cooling or wiping rust does not make it iron again.
Word model: not a balanced chemical equation.
Rusting is gradual; animation time is not real time.

steps.explanation: Cooling or wiping rust does not regenerate the original iron.

steps.question: Which result can cooling the remaining liquid wax produce?

choices.feedback: Melting and solidifying change state without making new substances.

choices.text: Turning carbon dioxide back into wax.
choices.feedback: Cooling the combustion products does not restore wax.

choices.text: Making all burnt wax reappear in the tray.
choices.feedback: Products include gases that spread into the air.

visual.description: A top row shows reversible wax melting and solidifying. A separate bottom row shows wax vapour plus oxygen forming carbon dioxide and water; these chemical products are not turned back into wax by cooling.
